results.title: Practical and ready-to-use methodology to assess the re-identification risk in anonymized datasets - PMC
results.content: This paper proposes a practical and ready-to-use methodology for re-identification risk assessment, the originality of which is manifold: (1) it is the first to follow well-known risk analysis methods (e.g. EBIOS) that have been used in the cybersecurity field for years, which consider not only the ability to perform an attack, but also the severity such an attack can have on an individual; (2) it is the first to qualify attributes and values of attributes with e.g. degree of exposure, as known real-world attacks mainly target certain types of attributes and not others; (3) it is the first to provide clear, comprehensible criteria and interpretable, explainable assessment results. From Section “Computing the severity (S)” to Section “Computing the re-identification risk”, we illustrate our methodological approach on a very simple initial dataset in Table 1 consisting of 12 rows and 6 columns, and its anonymized versions using two techniques—k-anonymity and HIPAA—presented in Tables 3 and 2, and we assess the risk of re-identification of the two anonymized datasets. Assessing an attacker’s ability to carry out these attacks is equivalent to assessing the exploitability of the quasi-identifiers, i.e. attribute types and values, available in the anonymized dataset to link the sensitive information to an individual. Let’s compute the likelihood, i.e. exploitability, for our two anonymized datasets k-anonymity and HIPAA by first assessing the exposure level of the attributes and the inference vulnerability. As shown in bold, for the k-anonymity dataset, the highest risk corresponds to an attacker using the combined attributes “Age”, “Gender” and “Country”, or the individual attributes “Age” or “Country” to “very easily” infer an individual’s “Disease” attribute, because the exploitability level of these attributes is classified as “4-Very Easy”. Based on this scale, the exploitability level of Tables 8, 9, 10 and 11, which provides information about an attacker’s ability to infer the “Disease” attribute value and the severity level of Tables 12 and 13, which is the maximum for the “Disease” attribute, we assess the risk of re-identification for each anonymized dataset: k-anonymity (Table 12) and HIPAA (Table 13).

results.title: Re-Identification Risk in HIPAA De-Identified Datasets: The MVA Attack - PMC
results.content: Patients in a significant MVA resulting in either permanent injury, hospitalization or death (for any victim) should have the accident location information omitted due to the significant risk of re-identification of HIPAA de-identified data. Accordingly, details of motor vehicle accidents and the resulting injuries are ubiquitous in medical records, especially in New York State, due to the requirement under the “No-Fault” law that insurance companies cover MVA related medical expenses regardless of accident “fault.” Given a de-identified database of free-text outpatient notes from the Buffalo area, it should be possible to re-identify some of them by linking them to newspaper articles from the same area, such as those published in the Buffalo News. Patients in a significant MVA resulting in either permanent injury, hospitalization or death (for any victim) should have the accident location information omitted due to the significant risk of re-identification of HIPAA de-identified data.
